mainTopic: Overcharging exceptions under רבי יהודה, then אונאת דברים (wronging with words) and how serious public shaming is.
overview: The עמוד opens with רבי יצחק בר אבא objecting that a ברייתא about a false שבועה over קדשים seems backwards. He then explains that each half of the ruling comes from a different phrase in the פסוק. Next the גמרא explains רבי יהודה's view in the משנה that a ספר תורה, a pearl, and an animal have no אונאה, and אמימר sets a limit on how far the price may be off. רבי יהודה בן בתירא adds that a horse, sword, or helmet sold during war also has no אונאה. A new משנה then teaches that there is also אונאה with words, such as reminding a בעל תשובה of his past. A ברייתא proves this from the פסוק 'לא תונו איש את עמיתו' and lists more examples, ending with רבי יהודה's warning that even acting interested in merchandise you cannot buy is forbidden. Three אמוראים explain why אונאת דברים is worse than אונאת ממון. The גמרא then teaches that shaming someone in public is like spilling blood, and that whoever does it goes down to גיהנם and never comes up. The עמוד ends by introducing a new teaching of רבה בר בר חנה in the name of רבי יוחנן, which continues on the next עמוד.

steps.title: The opposite makes more sense
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק בר אבא objects that the ruling in the ברייתא about קדשים seems backwards.
steps.simpleTranslation: The opposite is more reasonable!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יצחק בר אבא has just heard a ברייתא recited: for קדשים you are responsible for, a false שבועה makes you liable, and for קדשים you are not responsible for, you are exempt. He says it should be the other way around.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His logic is about the words 'against the Lord' in the פסוק. קדשים you are not responsible for belong more fully to ה', so they should be the ones that make you liable. The ones you are responsible for are partly still yours, so the ברייתא looks reversed.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense, it is reasonable

phrases.english: The opposite is reasonable!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיפְּכָא מִסְתַּבְּרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ברייתא recited just before this section.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's ruling: liable for קדשים he is responsible for, exempt for those he is not.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: קדשים he is not responsible for belong more to ה', so 'against the Lord' should make them the liable case. The ruling therefore looks reversed.

steps.title: Should I erase it?
steps.stepSummary: The תנא asks whether he should remove the ברייתא from what he recites.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Should I erase it?
steps.whatsHappening: The תנא who recited the ברייתא asks whether he should delete it, since it seems to have the wrong reading. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A תנא's job was to memorize and recite ברייתות word for word. If a ברייתא is wrong, he would stop reciting it. His question forces רבי יצחק בר אבא to say either that the text is mistaken or that it can be explained.

keyTerms.meaning: Should I erase it? Should I delete it?

phrases.english: He said to him: Should I erase it?
phrases.notes: The תנא who recited the ברייתא is the one asking here.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אֶיסְמְיַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to the objection by asking whether the text should be removed.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the ברייתא is a mistaken text that should be deleted.

steps.title: No, each half comes from a different phrase
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק בר אבא keeps the ברייתא. Liability comes from 'against the Lord', and the exemption comes from 'with his neighbor'.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: No. This is what it means. For קדשים he is responsible for, he is liable, because they are included by 'against the Lord, and deals falsely.' For קדשים he is not responsible for, he is exempt, because they are excluded by 'with his neighbor, and deals falsely.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יצחק בר אבא tells the תנא not to delete the ברייתא. He explains it by pointing to two different phrases in the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'against the Lord' adds קדשים that still have a link to ה' and also to the owner, because he must replace them. The phrase 'his neighbor' requires that the item be at least partly a person's property. קדשים he is not responsible for belong only to ה' and are not his at all, so they are left out.

keyTerms.meaning: Responsibility to replace something if it is lost
They are included (by a word in the פסוק)
It is excluded (by a word in the פסוק)

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא stands. Both phrases are needed: 'against the Lord' adds קדשים that still belong partly to the owner, and 'his neighbor' leaves out קדשים that belong to ה' alone.

phrases.english: He said to him: No.
This is what it is saying:
Sacrificial animals he is responsible for: he is liable,
since they are included by 'against the Lord, and deals falsely.'
And those he is not responsible for: he is exempt,
since they are excluded by 'with his neighbor, and deals falsely.'
phrases.notes: Same פסוק. 'His neighbor' means the item has to be at least partly a person's property.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: לָא. הָכִי קָאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the תנא's question and resolves the objection from step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Each half of the ruling is tied to a different phrase in the פסוק.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Against the Lord' should make קדשים that are fully ה''s the liable case.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Against the Lord' adds קדשים still partly the owner's. 'His neighbor' leaves out קדשים that are fully ה''s.

steps.title: רבי יהודה's ruling in the משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: רבי יהודה says a ספר תורה, a pearl, and an animal have no אונאה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: Even one who sells a ספר תורה, a pearl, or an animal: they have no אונאה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new topic. It quotes רבי יהודה's line from the משנה so it can explain it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, overcharging or underpaying by a set amount counts as אונאה, and the deal can be challenged. רבי יהודה adds these three items to the list of things that are exceptions to that rule. A sale of them stays valid even when the price is off.

keyTerms.meaning: Overcharging or underpaying in a sale

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:

phrases.aramaic: אַף הַמּוֹכֵר סֵפֶר תּוֹרָה, מַרְגָּלִית וּבְהֵמָה,
phrases.english: Even one who sells a Torah scroll, a pearl, or an animal,
they are not subject to overcharging.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: אַף הַמּוֹכֵר סֵפֶר תּוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, unrelated to the קדשים discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A ספר תורה, a pearl, and an animal are exceptions to the rules of אונאה.

steps.title: The ברייתא gives רבי יהודה's reasons
steps.stepSummary: A ספר תורה has no fixed value. Pearls and animals are wanted to make matching pairs.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is taught in a ברייתא: רבי יהודה says, even one who sells a ספר תורה has no אונאה, because there is no limit to its value. An animal and a pearl have no אונאה because a person wants to pair them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that explains why רבי יהודה said what he did in the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two separate reasons. A ספר תורה is so precious that no price is 'too high'. With pearls and animals, a buyer wants one that matches what he already has, so he will gladly pay more than usual.

keyTerms.meaning: It is taught in a ברייתא
There is no limit to its value
To pair them, to make a match

phrases.english: It is taught: Rabbi Yehuda says:
Even one who sells a Torah scroll,
it is not subject to overcharging,
because there is no limit to its value.
An animal and a pearl are not subject to overcharging,
because a person wants to pair them.
phrases.notes: For example, an animal that matches another one for plowing together, or a pearl that matches another for jewelry.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא, רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the reasons for the ruling in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A ספר תורה is priceless. Animals and pearls are bought to make matching pairs, so price differences do not count.

steps.title: People want to pair everything
steps.stepSummary: חכמים object that the matching reason would apply to every item.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: But doesn't a person want to pair everything?
steps.whatsHappening: חכמים challenge רבי יהודה's second reason within the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If wanting a match cancels אונאה, the rule would never apply, because people often want matching things of all kinds. So the reason seems far too broad.

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't it so that...? (opens a challenge)

phrases.english: They said to him:
phrases.notes: 'They' are חכמים, still inside the ברייתא.

phrases.english: But doesn't a person want to pair everything?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ לוֹ: וַהֲלֹא הַכֹּל אָדָם רוֹצֶה לְזַוְּוגָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the pairing reason given in step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reason that animals and pearls have no אונאה because people want to pair them.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Every item can be wanted as a match, so the reason would cancel אונאה completely.

steps.title: Matching matters much more for these items
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains how רבי יהודה would answer: matching is important for these items and not for others.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יהודה? These are important to him, and those are not important to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what רבי יהודה would answer, and then gives the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wanting a match is not the same for every item. For an animal and a pearl, getting an exact match really matters to the buyer, so he does not mind the price. For ordinary goods it does not matter enough.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yehuda?
phrases.notes: The question is: how would he answer חכמים?

phrases.aramaic: הָנֵי חֲשִׁיבִי לֵיהּ, וְהָנֵי לָא חֲשִׁיבִי לֵיהּ.
phrases.english: These are important to him, and those are not important to him.
phrases.notes: 'These' are animals and pearls. 'Those' are all other goods.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה, הָנֵי חֲשִׁיבִי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends רבי יהודה against the objection from חכמים.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishes between items by how much a match matters.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any wish to pair items would cancel אונאה.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only items where a match is really important, like animals and pearls, are left out of אונאה.

steps.title: How far can the price be off?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how big a price difference is allowed under רבי יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And up to how much?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the limit of רבי יהודה's rule. This sets up אמימר's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if these items have no normal אונאה, it is hard to believe any price at all is acceptable. So the גמרא wants to know where the line is.

phrases.english: And up to how much?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְעַד כַּמָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the limits of the rule that was just defended.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The largest price difference allowed for items that have no אונאה.

steps.title: אמימר: up to their full value
steps.stepSummary: אמימר rules that the price can be off by up to the full value of the item.
steps.simpleTranslation: אמימר said: Up to their value.
steps.whatsHappening: אמימר answers the question and sets the limit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being off by an amount as large as the item's whole value, meaning double the price, is still allowed. Going beyond that is too much even for these items.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who gives the limit here
Up to the amount of their value

steps.whatToRemember: For רבי יהודה, a ספר תורה, an animal, and a pearl have no normal אונאה. Still, according to אמימר, the price can only be off by up to the item's full value.
steps.confusionAlert: 'Up to their value' does not mean the fair price. It means the extra amount can be as large as the value itself, so the total can reach double.

phrases.english: Ameimar said: Up to their value.
phrases.notes: He means the price can be off by as much as the whole value, so up to double.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַמֵּימָר: עַד כְּדֵי דְּמֵיהֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from step 8.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The price may be off by up to the full value of the item.

steps.title: Wartime gear also has no overcharging law
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה בן בתירא adds that a horse, sword, or helmet sold during war has no אונאה, because life depends on them.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא teaches: רבי יהודה בן בתירא says that even someone who sells a horse, a sword, or a helmet during a war is not covered by the laws of overcharging, because these items can save a person's life.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that adds more items to the list of things with no אונאה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier the list had items like a ספר תורה, animals, and pearls. רבי יהודה בן בתירא adds wartime gear for a new reason: in battle, a person would pay any price for something that might save his life. So there is no fair 'market price' to measure overcharging against.

keyTerms.meaning: Overcharging or underpaying; wronging someone in a sale
A person's life; something life depends on

steps.whatToRemember: Items whose value cannot be fixed, whether because they are holy, wanted in matching pairs, or because life depends on them in war, are not covered by the laws of אונאה.

phrases.aramaic: תַּנְיָא, רַבִּי יְהוּדָה בֶּן בְּתֵירָא אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: It was taught in a ברייתא: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira says:

phrases.aramaic: אַף הַמּוֹכֵר סוּס וְסַיִיף וַחֲטִיטוֹם בַּמִּלְחָמָה –
phrases.english: Even one who sells a horse, a sword, or a helmet during wartime,
they are not subject to the law of overcharging,
because a person's life depends on them.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא, רַבִּי יְהוּדָה בֶּן בְּתֵירָא אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After finishing the discussion of how far the price may be off under רבי יהודה, the גמרא adds one more opinion expanding the list of items with no אונאה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A horse, sword, or helmet sold in wartime has no אונאה because life depends on it.

steps.title: The משנה teaches wronging with words
steps.stepSummary: Just as there is wronging in buying and selling, there is wronging with words. Examples: asking a price with no plan to buy, reminding a בעל תשובה of his past, or reminding a child of converts of his parents' past.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: Just as there is wronging in buying and selling, so there is wronging with words. A person should not ask a seller 'How much is this?' if he has no intention to buy. If someone did תשובה, do not say to him 'Remember what you used to do.' If someone is a child of converts, do not say to him 'Remember what your ancestors did,' as the פסוק says: 'Do not wrong a גר and do not oppress him.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It moves from money wronging to a new topic: hurting people with words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says that אונאה is not only about prices. Words that cause someone pain or false hope are also a kind of אונאה. Its first example even comes from the marketplace (asking a price for nothing), and then it moves to personal hurt (a person's past or family background).

keyTerms.meaning: Wronging with words; hurting someone through speech
Someone who has done תשובה and left his old ways

steps.confusionAlert: Asking 'How much is this?' is not forbidden in itself. It is only forbidden when you have no plan to buy, because you are raising the seller's hopes for nothing.

phrases.english: MISHNAH: Just as there is wronging in buying and selling,
so there is wronging with words.

phrases.aramaic: לֹא יֹאמַר לוֹ: בְּכַמָּה חֵפֶץ זֶה?
phrases.english: One may not say to him: How much is this item?
when he does not want to buy it.
If someone was a penitent,

phrases.aramaic: לֹא יֹאמַר לוֹ: זְכוֹר מַעֲשֶׂיךָ הָרִאשׁוֹנִים.
phrases.english: one may not say to him: Remember your earlier deeds.
If he is a child of converts,

phrases.aramaic: לֹא יֹאמַר לוֹ: זְכוֹר מַעֲשֵׂה אֲבוֹתֶיךָ,
phrases.english: one may not say to him: Remember the deeds of your ancestors,
as it is said: "And a convert you shall not wrong, nor oppress him."

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּשֵׁם שֶׁאוֹנָאָה בְּמִקָּח וּמִמְכָּר, כָּךְ אוֹנָאָה בִּדְבָרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה and a new topic, moving from money wronging to wronging with words.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There is a prohibition of אונאה with words, just as with money.

steps.title: The פסוק 'Do not wrong one another' is about words
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא states that the פסוק 'לא תונו איש את עמיתו' is talking about wronging with words.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: The רבנן taught: 'You shall not wrong one another.' This פסוק is talking about wronging with words.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that gives the source for the משנה's rule about wronging with words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא first states its claim: this פסוק refers to hurting with words. In the next steps it will ask how we know that and prove it.

phrases.english: GEMARA: The Rabbis taught:
"You shall not wrong one another,"
the verse is speaking about wronging with words.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: לֹא תוֹנוּ אִישׁ אֶת עֲמִיתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source in the תורה for the משנה's rule of אונאה with words.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'לא תונו איש את עמיתו' refers to wronging with words.

steps.title: Maybe the פסוק is about money instead?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks: how do we know this פסוק is about words and not about money wronging?
steps.simpleTranslation: Do you say it is about wronging with words? Maybe it is only about wronging with money?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא asks how we know its claim is right. It raises the possibility that the פסוק is really about money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'תונו' is the same word used for overcharging in a sale. So it is reasonable to think this פסוק is also about money. The ברייתא needs to show why that reading is not correct.

keyTerms.meaning: Do you say... or is it only... (a standard way to test a reading)

phrases.english: Do you say it is about wronging with words,
or is it only about wronging with money?

steps.triggerLanguage: אַתָּה אוֹמֵר בְּאוֹנָאַת דְּבָרִים, אוֹ אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא בְּאוֹנָאַת מָמוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the claim just made by suggesting the פסוק could mean money wronging.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How do we know 'לא תונו איש את עמיתו' is about words and not money?

steps.title: Money wronging already has its own פסוק
steps.stepSummary: Since an earlier פסוק already covers wronging in buying and selling, this second פסוק must be about wronging with words.
steps.simpleTranslation: When the תורה says 'And if you sell something to your fellow, or buy from your fellow,' wronging with money is already stated there. So what does 'You shall not wrong one another' teach? It must be about wronging with words.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers its own question by pointing to a different פסוק that already covers money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier פסוק (ויקרא 25:14) speaks openly about selling and buying, so it covers money wronging. The תורה does not repeat itself for nothing, so the second 'לא תונו' must teach something new: wronging with words.

keyTerms.meaning: So how do I fulfill (what does this פסוק teach)?

steps.whatToRemember: There are two 'לא תונו' פסוקים: one is about money (buying and selling), and the other is about words.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source in the תורה for the whole איסור of אונאת דברים, which the rest of the sugya builds on.

phrases.english: When it says
"And if you sell something to your fellow
or buy from your fellow's hand,"
wronging with money is already stated!
So how do I fulfill
"You shall not wrong one another"?
It is about wronging with words.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּשֶׁהוּא אוֹמֵר וְכִי תִמְכְּרוּ מִמְכָּר לַעֲמִיתֶךָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the question of step 13.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Money wronging is already written in ויקרא 25:14, so ויקרא 25:17 must refer to wronging with words.

steps.title: Examples of wronging with words
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא gives examples: do not remind a בעל תשובה of his past, do not remind a child of converts of his ancestors, and do not shame a גר who comes to learn תורה about what he used to eat.
steps.simpleTranslation: How so? If someone did תשובה, do not say to him 'Remember what you used to do.' If someone is a child of converts, do not say 'Remember what your ancestors did.' If a גר comes to learn תורה, do not say to him: 'A mouth that ate נבילות and טריפות, disgusting creatures and creeping things, comes to learn the תורה that was said by ה׳ Himself?'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא now explains in practice what wronging with words looks like.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first two examples match the משנה. The ברייתא adds a third one: mocking a גר who wants to learn תורה by bringing up the non-kosher food he used to eat. All three examples involve using a person's past to shame him.

keyTerms.meaning: Animals not slaughtered properly, and animals with fatal wounds
From the mouth of the Almighty

phrases.english: How so?

phrases.aramaic: אִם הָיָה בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה, אַל יֹאמַר לוֹ:
phrases.english: If someone was a penitent, one should not say to him:
"Remember your earlier deeds."

phrases.aramaic: אִם הָיָה בֶּן גֵּרִים, אַל יֹאמַר לוֹ:
phrases.english: If he was a child of converts, one should not say to him:
"Remember the deeds of your ancestors."

phrases.aramaic: אִם הָיָה גֵּר וּבָא לִלְמוֹד תּוֹרָה,
phrases.english: If he was a convert and came to learn Torah,

phrases.aramaic: אַל יֹאמַר לוֹ: ״פֶּה שֶׁאָכַל נְבֵילוֹת וּטְרֵיפוֹת,
phrases.english: one should not say to him: "A mouth that ate unslaughtered and fatally wounded animals,
disgusting creatures and creeping things,

phrases.aramaic: בָּא לִלְמוֹד תּוֹרָה שֶׁנֶּאֶמְרָה מִפִּי הַגְּבוּרָה״?
phrases.english: comes to learn Torah that was said from the mouth of the Almighty?"
phrases.notes: 'הגבורה' literally means 'the Power.' It is a name for ה׳.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא כֵּיצַד? אִם הָיָה בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After proving that the פסוק is about words, the ברייתא shows what that איסור looks like in real life.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Reminding a person of a shameful past (his own, his family's, or a גר's old eating habits) is אונאת דברים.

steps.title: Do not tell a suffering person that he must have sinned
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: when someone is suffering, sick, or burying his children, do not speak to him the way איוב's friends did.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone is going through suffering, illness, or the death of his children, do not tell him what איוב's friends told איוב: 'Your fear of God should have protected you. Did an innocent person ever die?'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא from step 15 keeps listing kinds of אונאת דברים. Here the example is hurting a person who is already in pain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: איוב's friends hinted that his troubles proved he had sinned. Saying this to someone who is suffering adds pain with words, so it counts as אונאת דברים.

keyTerms.meaning: Job, the righteous man who suffered greatly

phrases.english: If sufferings were coming upon him,
if illnesses were coming upon him,
or if he was burying his children,
one should not say to him
the way his friends spoke to Iyov:
"Is not your fear [of God] your confidence,
your hope the innocence of your ways?

phrases.aramaic: זְכׇר נָא מִי הוּא נָקִי אָבָד״.
phrases.english: Remember, please, who ever perished being innocent?"

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם הָיוּ יִסּוּרִין בָּאִין עָלָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another example to the ברייתא's list from step 15.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: It is forbidden to tell a suffering person that his suffering comes from his sins.

steps.title: Do not send buyers to someone who never sells
steps.stepSummary: Do not send donkey drivers looking for grain to a person you know has never sold grain.
steps.simpleTranslation: If donkey drivers ask you for grain, do not tell them 'Go to so-and-so, he sells grain' when you know he has never sold any.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives one more example of אונאת דברים, this time a trick that wastes people's time and embarrasses them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No money is lost here, but the buyers are sent on a pointless trip and the other man is bothered for nothing. Hurting people with words alone is enough to count as אונאת דברים.

keyTerms.meaning: donkey drivers, merchants who carry goods on donkeys

phrases.english: If donkey drivers were
asking him for grain,
he should not say to them:
"Go to so-and-so, because he sells grain,"
when he knows that the man never sold [grain].

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם הָיוּ חַמָּרִים מְבַקְּשִׁין תְּבוּאָה מִמֶּנּוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of examples in the ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sending people on purpose to someone who cannot help them is אונאת דברים.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: do not even look at merchandise you cannot buy
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה adds that one should not even act interested in merchandise when he has no money, because only the heart knows the real intent, and about such matters the תורה says 'ויראת מאלהיך'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: you should not even look at an item as if you want to buy it when you have no money. Only your heart knows what you really mean, and for anything that depends on the heart, the תורה says 'And you shall fear your God'.
steps.whatsHappening: Inside the same ברייתא, רבי יהודה goes further than the earlier examples: even a look, with no words at all, can mislead a seller.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nobody else can see whether a person truly meant to buy, so it is hard for people to catch. That is why the תורה adds 'ויראת מאלהיך': God knows what is in your heart.

keyTerms.meaning: set his eyes on, look at with interest
given over to the heart, known only to the person himself
and you shall fear your God

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the next step: the phrase 'ויראת מאלהיך' becomes רבי שמעון בן יוחאי's proof that אונאת דברים is more serious.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:

phrases.aramaic: אַף לֹא יִתְלֶה עֵינָיו עַל הַמִּקָּח,
phrases.english: one should not even set his eyes on merchandise
at a time when he has no money,
since the matter is given over to the heart,
and any matter given over to the heart,
about it is said: "And you shall fear your God."
phrases.notes: ויקרא 25:17, the same פסוק of 'לא תונו' from step 12.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: אַף לֹא יִתְלֶה עֵינָיו עַל הַמִּקָּח
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Widens the rule: even a misleading look, not only words, is included.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Acting interested in buying without the money to buy is forbidden; God, who knows the heart, holds a person responsible.

steps.title: Wronging with words is worse because the תורה says 'fear your God'
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחאי: אונאת דברים is greater than אונאת ממון, because only it has 'ויראת מאלהיך' written about it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Hurting someone with words is a bigger sin than cheating him with money. The proof is that the תורה wrote 'And you shall fear your God' about words, and not about money.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא is finished. Now an אמורא compares the two kinds of wronging and says words are worse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The extra phrase 'ויראת מאלהיך' appears only by the פסוק about words. רבי שמעון בן יוחאי reads this as a sign that the תורה treats it more seriously.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַאי:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai:
Wronging with words is greater than wronging with money,
for about this one it is said: "And you shall fear your God,"
and about that one it is not said: "And you shall fear your God."

steps.triggerLanguage: גָּדוֹל אוֹנָאַת דְּבָרִים מֵאוֹנָאַת מָמוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the phrase 'ויראת מאלהיך' from step 18 to rank the two kinds of wronging.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אונאת דברים is more serious than אונאת ממון, based on the extra words 'ויראת מאלהיך'.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר: words hurt the person himself
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר gives another reason: wronging with words hurts the person himself, while wronging with money only hurts his money.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר says: this one (words) hurts the person's body, and that one (money) only hurts his wallet.
steps.whatsHappening: A second אמורא gives his own reason why אונאת דברים is worse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר does not use the פסוק. His reason is common sense: harming a person himself is worse than harming his possessions.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Elazar says:
This is against his body, and that is against his money.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר: זֶה בְּגוּפוֹ וְזֶה בְּמָמוֹנוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A different reason for the same idea as step 19.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Words are worse because they hurt the person himself, not just his belongings.

steps.title: רבי שמואל בר נחמני: money can be returned, words cannot
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמואל בר נחמני gives a third reason: money that was overcharged can be returned, but hurtful words cannot be taken back.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמואל בר נחמני says: this one (money) can be paid back, but that one (words) can never be paid back.
steps.whatsHappening: A third אמורא explains why אונאת דברים is worse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If you overcharged, you can give the extra money back and the damage is fixed. Hurt and shame cannot be fully undone.

keyTerms.meaning: can be given back, can be repaid

steps.whatToRemember: There are three reasons why אונאת דברים is worse than אונאת ממון: the תורה adds 'ויראת מאלהיך' (רבי שמעון בן יוחאי), it hurts the person himself (רבי אלעזר), and it cannot be undone (רבי שמואל בר נחמני).

phrases.english: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said:
This can be given back,
phrases.notes: Careful: here 'this' means the money wronging, the opposite order from the last two steps.

phrases.english: and that cannot be given back.

steps.triggerLanguage: זֶה נִיתַּן לְהִישָּׁבוֹן, וְזֶה לֹא נִיתַּן לְהִישָּׁבוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third reason for the same idea as steps 19 and 20.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Words are worse because the damage cannot be repaid.

steps.title: Shaming someone in public is like spilling blood
steps.stepSummary: A תנא taught in front of רב נחמן בר יצחק: anyone who shames his friend in public is like someone who spills blood.
steps.simpleTranslation: A תנא taught before רב נחמן בר יצחק: whoever makes his friend's face go white in public is as if he spilled blood.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a teaching about how serious one kind of hurtful speech is: public embarrassment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Whitening the face' is the expression for shaming someone. The teaching compares it to murder, which shows how serious the sin is.

keyTerms.meaning: here, the one in the study hall who memorized and recited ברייתות
one who 'whitens' his friend's face, meaning shames him

phrases.aramaic: תָּנֵי תַּנָּא קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק:
phrases.english: A tanna taught before Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak:
Anyone who whitens his friend's face in public
is as if he spills blood.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנֵי תַּנָּא קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from ranking words over money to how severe public shaming is.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Publicly embarrassing someone is like murder.

steps.title: רב נחמן בר יצחק agrees: the red leaves and the white comes
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק agrees with the תנא, because you can see the red drain from the shamed person's face and paleness take its place.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said to him: You said it well. We see that the red goes away and the white comes, as if his blood was spilled.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק supports the teaching from step 22 with something anyone can see.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A shamed person first blushes red, then turns pale. The blood leaving his face looks like a kind of bloodshed, so the comparison to murder fits.

phrases.english: He said to him: You are saying well,
for we see him,
that the red goes away and the white comes.

steps.triggerLanguage: שַׁפִּיר קָא אָמְרַתְּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the teaching of step 22.
steps.raayaObject: That shaming someone in public is like spilling blood.
steps.raayaSupportSource: What we see happen: the shamed person's face goes from red to pale.

steps.title: אביי asks what people in ארץ ישראל are careful about
steps.stepSummary: אביי asks רב דימי which מצוה the people of ארץ ישראל are especially careful with.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to רב דימי: In the West, what are they especially careful about?
steps.whatsHappening: אביי asks a question, and the answer in the next step brings us back to shaming people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב דימי traveled between ארץ ישראל and בבל, so אביי asks him about the practices there. This sets up the answer in step 25.

phrases.english: Abaye said to Rav Dimi:
In the West, what are they careful about?
phrases.notes: 'The West' means ארץ ישראל, which is west of בבל.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּמַעְרְבָא בְּמַאי זְהִירִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a short exchange that will connect back to public shaming.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which מצוה the people of ארץ ישראל are especially careful about.

steps.title: They are careful not to shame people
steps.stepSummary: רב דימי answers that they are careful not to embarrass others, and he brings רבי חנינא's teaching that everyone goes down to גיהנם except three.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: They are careful not to make people's faces go white, because רבי חנינא said: Everyone goes down to גיהנם except for three.
steps.whatsHappening: רב דימי answers אביי and gives the source for this care: רבי חנינא's teaching. The list of the three comes right after this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The people of ארץ ישראל took shaming people so seriously because of רבי חנינא's teaching. The rest of it, which comes next, shows how harsh the punishment for shaming is.

keyTerms.meaning: גיהנם, the place of punishment after death

steps.confusionAlert: 'Everyone goes down to גיהנם' sounds shocking. The teaching is only beginning here, and the next lines explain who the three are and why it matters.

phrases.english: He said to him: About whitening faces,
as Rabbi Chanina said:
Everyone goes down to Gehinnom, except for three.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: בְּאַחְווֹרֵי אַפֵּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's question from step 24.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: In ארץ ישראל they are careful not to shame others, based on רבי חנינא's teaching about גיהנם.

steps.title: Does everyone really go down to גיהנם?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the wording of רבי חנינא's statement that 'everyone' goes down to גיהנם.
steps.simpleTranslation: Can you really think that everyone goes down to גיהנם?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the words of רבי חנינא from the last step. Taken literally, they would mean that every single person goes down to גיהנם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying that everyone, including righteous people, goes to גיהנם makes no sense. So the גמרא shows that the plain wording cannot be right as it stands. This prepares the ground for a corrected reading in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Your mind; together, 'would it enter your mind?'

phrases.english: Does it enter your mind that everyone goes down?

steps.triggerLanguage: הַכֹּל סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the literal wording of רבי חנינא's statement quoted by רב דימי.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי חנינא's statement that everyone goes down to גיהנם except three
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: It cannot be that every person, even the righteous, goes down to גיהנם, so the statement cannot be read literally.

steps.title: Corrected reading: three who go down and never come up
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rereads רבי חנינא: everyone who goes down to גיהנם eventually comes up, except three kinds of sinners who never come up.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say this: Everyone who goes down to גיהנם comes up again, except for three who go down and do not come up. These are: one who sins with a married woman, one who shames his friend in public, and one who calls his friend by an insulting name.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the reading of רבי חנינא's statement. It is not that everyone goes down. Rather, whoever goes down eventually comes out, except for three people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The exception is no longer about who goes down. It is about who stays there forever. Two of the three sins on the list are about shaming people, which fits רב דימי's point that ארץ ישראל was careful about embarrassing others.

keyTerms.meaning: The place of punishment after death
Shames his friend in public (literally, makes his face turn white)
Calls someone by an insulting nickname

steps.whatToRemember: Shaming someone in public and calling someone an insulting name are listed together with adultery as sins whose doers go down to גיהנם and do not come up.

phrases.english: Rather, say:
All who go down to גיהנם come up,
except for three who go down and do not come up.
And these are they:
one who has relations with a married woman,
and one who shames his friend in public,
and one who calls his friend by an insulting name.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אֵימָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by rereading רבי חנינא's statement.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Everyone goes down to גיהנם except three.
steps.terutzMaskana: Everyone who goes down to גיהנם eventually comes up, except three who never come up.

steps.title: Isn't calling names the same as shaming?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the insulting-nickname caller is listed separately, since that seems to be the same as shaming someone.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who calls his friend an insulting name: isn't that the same as one who shames him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא notices that two items on the list look like the same thing. It asks why they are counted as two separate sins.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Calling someone an insulting name is a way of shaming him. If so, the list seems to repeat itself, and it should only have two items. The גמרא wants to know what the extra item adds.

phrases.english: One who calls names: isn't that the same as one who shames?

steps.triggerLanguage: מְכַנֶּה הַיְינוּ מַלְבִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the list of three that was just set up.
steps.kashyaTarget: The list of three in רבי חנינא's corrected statement
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Calling a friend an insulting name is itself shaming him, so listing it separately seems to repeat the same sin.

steps.title: Even when the victim is already used to the nickname
steps.stepSummary: The nickname-caller is listed separately because he is punished even when the victim is so used to the name that he no longer feels shamed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even though the person has grown used to being called by that name.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the nickname-caller is a separate case. He is guilty even if the nickname no longer embarrasses the victim, because he has gotten used to it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The one who shames is guilty because the victim actually feels the embarrassment. The nickname-caller is guilty even when no shame is felt anymore, because he means to insult. That is why he needs his own place on the list.

keyTerms.meaning: Trampled; used so much that it is worn in
With his name, as his regular name

steps.whatToRemember: Insulting nicknames are a serious sin even when the victim no longer seems hurt by them.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the nickname is fine once the person 'doesn't mind anymore.' The גמרא lists this case separately exactly to say that he is still guilty.

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל גַּב דְּדָשׁ בֵּיהּ בִּשְׁמֵיהּ.
phrases.english: Even though he has grown used to it as his name.
phrases.notes: דָּשׁ literally means 'trampled.' The nickname has been used so much that it feels like his real name.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַף עַל גַּב דְּדָשׁ בֵּיהּ בִּשְׁמֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers why the name-caller is a separate case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing that the case goes further than the one before it
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Calling names is just one kind of shaming, so it is counted twice.
steps.terutzMaskana: The name-caller is guilty even when the victim no longer feels shamed, so it is a separate case.

steps.title: Introducing a teaching of רבה בר בר חנה in the name of רבי יוחנן
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens a new statement that רבה בר בר חנה says in the name of רבי יוחנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר בר חנה says that רבי יוחנן says:
steps.whatsHappening: This line is a setup. It names who is about to speak, and the actual teaching comes right after this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This line only tells us the chain of teachers. רבי יוחנן taught it, and רבה בר בר חנה passed it on. The content of the teaching comes on the next עמוד.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who passes on many teachings of רבי יוחנן
A leading אמורא of ארץ ישראל

phrases.english: Rabba bar bar Ḥana says
that Rabbi Yoḥanan says:

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new statement after the discussion of the three sinners is finished.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only the speakers are named here; the content of the teaching comes next.
